{"id": "277b674d-341c-42c5-8eb5-2c168aded65a", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Switching to Elastic throughput is a single setting change. It doesn't cause application downtime.

**Console**
1. Open the EFS console and select your file system.
2. Choose **Edit** in the General settings section.
3. Under **Throughput mode**, select **Enhanced**, then **Elastic**.
4. Save your changes.

**AWS CLI**
```
aws efs update-file-system \
  --file-system-id fs-xxxxxxxx \
  --throughput-mode elastic
```
If the file system is on Provisioned mode, you don't need to pass the provisioned amount. Elastic ignores it.

**Things to know before switching**
- **24-hour lock:** If you recently switched to Provisioned or raised the provisioned amount, you can't move to Elastic until 24 hours have passed. If the call fails with an error about changing throughput mode, this is likely why.
- **Billing:** Elastic bills per GB of data read and written, not per provisioned MiBps. It suits spiky or unpredictable workloads. If your workload drives steady, high throughput, Provisioned can cost less.
- **Cost guardrails:** AWS recommends a CloudWatch alarm on `MeteredIOBytes` so a runaway workload doesn't surprise you on cost.
- **Performance mode:** Elastic requires the General Purpose performance mode. File systems on Max I/O can't use it.

I checked us-east-1 in this account (012345678901_1) and found no EFS file systems. Yours may be in another region or account. If you give me the region and file system ID, I can confirm its current mode, performance mode and any recent changes. I can also check CloudWatch throughput metrics to confirm that throughput is what's limiting you. Low throughput on Bursting mode often comes from an exhausted burst credit balance. Elastic fixes that.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
